I believe that our current definition of docs#EMetricSpace is broken (same with docs#PseudoEMetricSpace). We require that the topology (and uniformity) of the space is defined by the distance. In particular, points with distance ∞ from every other point must be isolated points.

I think this is highly undesirable in practice. For example, ℝ≥0∞ is not an EMetricSpace, since ∞ is not an isolated point. In fact, we have no instances of PseudoEMetricSpace besides instances that come from PseudoMetricSpace or instances that already assume (Pseudo)EMetricSpace on some other type.

I'm not sure how to best "fix" this. Presumably there's a bunch of lemmas that require EMetricSpace and talk about the topology of the space? (If not, we can simply remove the uniformity from the data of an EMetricSpace.)
I would like ℝ≥0∞ to be an EMetricSpace (if it isn't, then what is?), but I think it cannot be equipped with a nice uniformity? If so, then we should just remove the uniformity from EMetricSpace. However, we want it to work well with the topology (I think), so maybe we should redefine PseudoEMetricSpace to include an axiom that the topology plays well with edist something like this

def EMetric.ball [EDist α] (x : α) (ε : ℝ≥0∞) : Set α :=
  { y | edist y x < ε }

class PseudoEMetricSpace (α : Type u) [TopologicalSpace α] extends EDist α : Type u where
  edist_self : ∀ x : α, edist x x = 0
  edist_comm : ∀ x y : α, edist x y = edist y x
  edist_triangle : ∀ x y z : α, edist x z ≤ edist x y + edist y z
  isOpen_ball : ∀ (x : α) (r : ℝ≥0∞), IsOpen (EMetric.ball x r)

Maybe we want a stronger condition on the topology, e.g. that on all balls (also of infinite radius) the topology coincides with the topology given by edist, so that only the topology between the balls of infinite radius is left unspecified.

(I brought this up in the discussion of #21422)
I wouldn't call it "broken". There are 2 examples that work with our definition: Closeds and Lp emetric on the space of all measurable functions.
Is there a consensus in the literature on what should be called an extended metric space?
Definitely, we can have a typeclass between EDist and the current EMetricSpace. BTW, ENNReals won't be EMetricSpace in terms of your definition, because ball ∞ 1 isn't open.
+1 example: max edistance on functions that aren't assumed to be bounded.
+1: evariation on paths that aren't assumed to have bounded variation.
We can define EDist ENNReal, then see what properties are still true, then decide if we want to have a typeclass for this.
Maybe I am a bit too harsh with my words, but I'm wondering if we can weaken the type-class assumptions to make this class more widely useful.

Yury G. Kudryashov said:

I wouldn't call it "broken". There are 2 examples that work with our definition: Closeds and Lp emetric on the space of all measurable functions.

Both of these require that the space you start with is already an EMetricSpace, and in both cases (I think?) if you start with a metric space you get a metric space out. So that still doesn't provide any EMetric spaces used in Mathlib that are not Metric spaces.
In your extra examples, are the topologies given by the emetric-space actually useful though?
Closeds on the real line aren't a MetricSpace. E.g., the Hausdorff distance between {4 ^ n | n : Nat} and {2 * 4 ^ n | n : Nat} is infinity.

I don't think our definition is broken: it does exactly what it is designed for. The standard example is indeed L^p (even when the base space is a nice metric space): the edistance between two functions is the integral of |f - g|, which can be infinite. Two functions which are at infinite distance are really not comparable in any way, so you really want them to be in different connected components of the L^p space.

Thanks for your input! It's clear that I was wrong (sorry for the provocative title), and that EMetricSpace works fine. Maybe I'll investigate at some later point if there is a class between EDist and EMetricSpace where ENNReal fits nicely.

The reason I started this discussion is by PR #21422, where we add classes ENormedAddCommMonoid, which is supposed to be satisfied by both NormedAddCommGroup and ENNReal. NormedAddCommGroup is defined in terms of MetricSpace, so I was wondering to what extend we could have ENormedAddCommMonoid extend EMetricSpace.

Isn't what Floris is actually saying, that no amount of metric or emetric stuff with d(x,infty)=infty will ever give the right topology on ENNReal, which presumably is the topology making it homeomorphic to the closed interval.

So somehow maybe the conclusion is that ENNReal should not actually be an emetric space, because this doesn't even give the right notion of convergence, e.g. 1+1+1+1+1+1+... does not converge to infinity in the emetric, even though this is clearly desirable

I'm reviving this topic.

EMetricSpace is not broken, but we are using it for results that I would also like to have on ENNReal. For example docs#eVariationOn makes perfect sense for functions into ENNReal, and most basic properties should work exactly the same in that case. In fact, a student of mine, @Felix Pernegger wants to use eVariationOn for ENNReal.

Here is a concrete suggestion: we add two new classes, WeakEMetricSpace and WeakPseudoEMetricSpace (other name suggestions welcome) which both have type signature 

class ... (α : Type u) [TopologicalSpace α] : Type u

which have the axioms edist_self/edist_comm/edist_triangle(/eq_of_edist_eq_zero) and then some axioms that say that the topology is at least (EDIT: most) as fine as the topology given by edist, but not any finer coarser when restricted to a ball of finite radius. This has as notable new instances ENNReal and ENat.

We then try to go through Mathlib and see which results about (Pseudo)EMetricSpaces can be generalized to the weak version.

Two things I'm unsure about:

  1. How to most conveniently state the conditions on the topology that we want?
  2. Is there a natural UniformSpace structure on ENNReal? If so, could we instead have axioms stating "the uniform space structure on ENNReal is compatible with edist"?

How does this sound?
(Even if the answer to question 2 is unknown, I think we can go ahead with this proposal, and change it to use UniformSpace as the need arises.)

(cc @Yury G. Kudryashov @Sébastien Gouëzel @Michael Rothgang)
(reading back, this is working out what Yury suggested above)

I don't see any sensible uniform structure on ENNReal that is compatible with the topology, as it should allow very large reals to be close to infinity (as the topology does), which doesn't play well with the edist.

And I think your proposal to add WeakEMetricSpace is a very good idea!
ENNReal is compact, so it admits a unique uniform structure making it uniformly equivalent to the closed interval
the theorem is docs#unique_uniformity_of_compact
maybe you could restrict to sets with finite radius
#27756 (heavy work in progress) starts in this direction
#32891 (superseding #27756) is a PR from a student that I'm supervising which implements this.
This is great! I'll try to take a look at the PR very soon.

Consider the following metric definition for extended reals (the metric space for ENNReal is a sub-metric space of the metric space of full extended reals):

  1. dist (+inf,+inf) = 0
  2. dist (-inf,-inf) = 0
  3. dist (+inf, -int) = dist (-inf, +inf) = 1
  4. dist (+inf, r) = 1
  5. dist (-inf, r) = 1
  6. dist (r1, r2) = |r1 - r2| / (1 + |r1 - r2|)
    This is a metric space (the metric value is always finite, <= 1). The metric between finite reals is strictly less than 1. The metric between different infinities is 1, and between same infinites is 0. If dist(x,x) = 0, then x = x.
This is the metric space for extreals I constructed in HOL4.

I think we would still like to preserve the normal distance on ENNReal though, even if the topology of ENNReal is metrizable (which is not hard anyways, as it is homeomorphic to [0,1]); I don't see a benefit from having edist 2 0 = 2 / 3
I Agree, if we want to use that distance, why not just use the interval [0, 1] (and potentially the homeomorphism from [-\infty, \infty] to [0, 1]?

Floris van Doorn said:

I Agree, if we want to use that distance, why not just use the interval [0, 1] (and potentially the homeomorphism from [-\infty, \infty] to [0, 1]?

Let's call this homeomorphism a function contract which maps [-\infty, \infty] to [0, 1] (or maybe to [-1,1]). Are you saying the "distance" of two extended reals would be defined by edist (R1,R2) = |contract(R1) - contract(R2)| ? That's the choice of one author in Coq. I think it's problematic: the distance between a finite and infinite reals is not a fixed value, e.g. edist(1,+infty) != edist(2,+infty), which is counterintuitive.

In this metric, the sequence 0, 1, 2, 3, ... doesn't converge to infinity!

Oh sorry, I misread your actual distance function. Similar to what Aaron said, if we use this distance functions, ∞\infty∞ and −∞-\infty−∞ are isolated points (according to the topology induced by that distance), which is the wrong topology.
Also, if we want to do analysis, a property that would be nice to have is dist x 0 = ‖x‖. But under your definition, it would mean that ‖∞‖ = 1, which gives the wrong notion of integrability (c.f. docs#MeasureTheory.HasFiniteIntegral)

Hmmm, I think you (two) are right. The two isolated points (+/-infty) are indeed issues I met in some related proofs. The d/(1+d) shape is also a problem when handling Lipschitz conditions. Now I start to wonder if |contract(R1) - contract(R2)| a better way. Thanks any way.
btw #38105 is now merged and docs#WeakEMetricSpace / docs#WeakPseudoEMetricSpace exist

What about having a common class LawfulEDist with only edist_self, edist_comm and edist_triangle that both WeakPseudoEMetricSpace and PseudoEMetricSpace inherit from, so that lemmas that only mention those are not duplicated?

Lua Viana Reis said:

What about having a common class LawfulEDist with only edist_self, edist_comm and edist_triangle that both WeakPseudoEMetricSpace and PseudoEMetricSpace inherit from, so that lemmas that only mention those are not duplicated?

Isnt this redudant by PseudoEMetricSpace.toWeakPseudoEMetricSpace?
Then, perhaps PseudoEMetricSpace could inherit from WeakPseudoEMetricSpace with this instance being the default constructor? At least, this would make it easier to avoid instances diamonds, no?

I ask because I was trying to make ediam use this class, but reorganizing the EMetricSpace.Defs file to have the appropiate lemmas only depend on the weak notion seemed a bit complicated. If we don't want duplication, then WeakPseudoEMetricSpace would have to be defined before the lemmas for PseudoEMetricSpace

on a side note, if you're working on that code, might be a good opportunity to fix the typo in the description of docs#WeakPseudoEMetricSpace (at one point it says "at least as fine" and at another point it says "at most as fine")

Oh, we should definitely define WeakPseudoEMetricSpace before proving basic things about PseudoEMetricSpace. Lemmas like docs#edist_triangle_left should definitely be formulatated for the weak version, not for the strong version.

This is a temporary situation, since WeakPseudoEMetricSpace has been merged only recently, and we still need to adapt the library to actually use it.

Lua Viana Reis said:

What about having a common class LawfulEDist with only edist_self, edist_comm and edist_triangle that both WeakPseudoEMetricSpace and PseudoEMetricSpace inherit from, so that lemmas that only mention those are not duplicated?

I actually think this is a very good idea now;
Today I tried to generalise basic lemmas from PseudoEMetricSpace to WeakPseudoEMetricSpace, however WeakPseudoEMetricSpace requires a topological space as argument while PseudoEMetricSpace doesn't, thus the generalisation is a bit awkward. So LawfulEDist would be very natural here.

Having [LawfulEDist X] could be nice, but its use is not super clear to me that it's really useful.
Is there an advantage of having [LawfulEDist X] besides that it is shorter to write than [TopologicalSpace X] [WeakPseudoEMetricSpace X]? I guess it simplifies the statement of docs#uniformSpaceOfEDist...

For whom it may concern; all basic theory about docs#WeakPseudoEMetricSpace is now merged and one can generalize many/most results about docs#PseudoEMetricSpace relatively mechanically (which I did in #42662, #42688, #42741, ...). Of course these generalizations are best to be done "from the bottom up" w.r.t. the dependency graph.
